brief: A seven-cell honeycomb standing on at least three stud spikes facing down as feet.

requirements.evidence: Seven full hex bases: piece:0,0,0 in the middle and the six cells around it (0,-1; -1,0; 1,-1; -1,1; 1,0; 0,1), all on level 0, with outer faces capped and joints bolted.

requirements.requirement: Stands on at least three stud spikes facing down as feet
requirements.evidence: Six stud spikes facing down at level 0, one at each inner point where three cells meet (spike:0#-1,0|-1,1|0,0 and the other five). They are all close to the centre, about 96 mm out, so the outer cells overhang them.

finish.summary: I built a seven-cell honeycomb: one full hex base at 0,0 with six full bases around it, all on level 0. It stands on six stud spikes facing down, one at each of the six inner points where three cells meet. I also capped the 18 open outer faces and bolted the 12 joints between cells (30 parts plus the six feet). check_build passes with no issues and the collision check reads clear. One thing to know: these six points are the only places a downward stud spike is offered, so all the feet sit about 96 mm from the centre, under a build roughly 500 mm across. The outer cells hang out past the feet.

lines.label: M6 brass heat-set insert, 7.6 mm (initeq M6-1.0 Short)
M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
